newsitem.title: USA: USDA decides Friday if sugar quota goes up.
newsitem.headline: USDA decides Friday if sugar quota goes up.

text.p: The new formula for setting the U.S. sugar import quota faces its first test on Friday, dogged by doubts in the food and drink industry over whether it would result in a large enough sugar supply.
One trade group, the Sweetener Users Association, said it would ask Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman to raise the quota even if the formula ruled against it.
When it was adopted last fall, the formula was intended to make U.S. quota-setting clear and understandable to all sides, with three dates for possible changes.
The first opportunity comes Friday, based on the Agriculture Department's report on world crops.

Under the new system, sugar imports of 1.7 million tonnes have been allocated for fiscal 1997. An additional 200,000 tonnes would be authorized in January, March and May if USDA forecast a stocks-to-use ratio of 15.5 percent or less.
It replaced a system in which the Agriculture Department set a quota that could be adjusted at any time with no warning.
Analysts said they expected a close call Friday on the potential increase.

"If we don't get it, we are going to have to make the case to (Agriculture Secretary Glickman that) there are discretionary authorities built into this (formula)," said Tom Hammer of the Sweetener Users Association.

A month ago, USDA estimated a sugar ratio of 15.6 percent. Hammer said a change of a few thousand short tons, out of the 10.2 million short tons used annually, would open the door to the larger import quota. Without it, he said, U.S. supplies would be too tight for comfort.
Glickman retained power under the new formula to increase the quota if conditions warranted.

Dalton Yancy, spokesman for Florida and Texas sugar grower groups, pointed to a sizable increase in U.S. output -- up 150,000 short tons, or 136,077 tonnes in December from November -- and discounted fears of short supplies.
"Everybody's looking to see if USDA is going to do what it said it was going to do" by adopting the formula, Yancy said. "I think USDA's credibility is kind of on the line."
Despite sugar users' concerns about tight supplies, one analyst said the sugar stocks ratio fell to 13 percent for two years earlier this decade without much impact on domestic sugar prices.
The United States uses a loan program to assure growers of a minimum price for domestic sugar, and restricts imports.

Sugar growers and food companies generally supported the shift to a formula for setting the import quota. Each side tried to mold the formula to its advantage -- growers wanted a low stocks ratio before imports would be increase and foodmakers wanted large imports to constrain U.S. prices.
